name: Choice / Strategy
subtitle: Make critical choices under constraints of information and resources; the core is the presentation of information and the explainability of consequences.
demoRuleHint: Rule example: 2–3 visible options appear → the player selects one → a fixed cost and reward are generated → the situation updates → next round of choices.
problemsSolved: Eliminate 'pseudo-choices' caused by insufficient option differentiation.
Balance information disclosure and randomness to avoid pure guessing or pure arithmetic.
Support strategic depth through rounds and resource curves, preventing one-click endings.
Control information volume to prevent decision fatigue and excessive guessing.
Limit resources to increase strategic depth, avoiding shallow decisions caused by excess resources.
Balance the proportion of hidden information and number of visible options to enhance the player's ability to explain consequences.
learningGoals: Beginner: understand the decision loop — options presented → choose → cost & payoff → situation updates — and reproduce one pick-of-three in the demo
Intermediate: write the option-generation and consequence-settlement contract (payoff magnitude, reroll cost, info refresh rate), and learn to spot fake choices
Advanced: design information-disclosure ratios and risk visualization, and verify decision quality with option-pick distribution and per-option win-rate gaps
minimalRules: Information: number of visible options ≤ 3, proportion of hidden information ≤ 30%.
Resources: available resource amount per round ≤ 2, and no more than 2 resource types.
Consequences: state changes (rewards/punishments) resulting from each choice must be traceable and explainable, and the magnitude of change ≤ 20% of current resources.
Decision cost: each choice consumes a fixed cost, with cost-to-reward ratio ≤ 1:1; high cost limits choice frequency, increasing depth; low cost increases frequency, reducing depth.

Information update frequency: information updated per round ≤ 1/3 of current visible options; frequent updates increase adaptability, reducing planning depth; sparse updates increase planning depth, reducing adaptability.
A moderate proportion of hidden information can improve decision quality; too low leads to overanalysis, too high leads to decision fatigue.
systemLoopHint: Input (choice) → Check (resource sufficiency) → Feedback (reward/punishment) → State change (situation update) → New information → New input.

combos.effect: In a combat round, the player can choose to 'Attack' or 'Defend'. Attacking consumes 1 point of attack power, defending consumes 1 point of defense power; the choice determines the combat outcome path.
At the start of each round, 1–2 events are randomly drawn from an event pool; the player makes a choice based on the event content, and the event pool weights can be adjusted.
At the end of each season, the player chooses an upgrade path based on accumulated resources; the chosen path affects the rewards and visibility of subsequent options.

advancedWarnings: Insufficient option differentiation can lead to 'pseudo-choices'.
Unexplained consequences prevent players from learning and improving.
Excessive information fatigues newcomers; too little turns it into guessing.
Excessive randomization weakens the player's sense of strategic control.
advancedAlgoRefs: Events: event pool and weights, guaranteed events, and deduplication.
Economy: resource curves, inflation control, threshold design.

demoLab.title: Spotting Fake Choices
demoLab.action: Pick each of "Gain Gold" / "Buff Damage" / "Heal" once per round, tracking the net change in power and risk
demoLab.observe: If the three options converge in net value, the choice degenerates into a fake one. Watch which option wins long-term — option differences must land on explainable numbers, or players are just rolling dice

demoLab.title: Risk Accumulation Watch
demoLab.action: Pick only "Gain Gold" every round and watch the risk metric climb
demoLab.observe: A single-track strategy pushes risk up — short-term gains traded for long-term fragility. risk carries "explainable consequences": when every choice is traceable, players learn and improve instead of feeling the system is out to get them

demoLab.title: Reroll Cost Experiment
demoLab.action: Click "Reroll (secondary)" before choosing each round, and compare the power curve against never rerolling
demoLab.observe: Reroll trades a fixed cost for better options: when cost ≤ benefit it is the rational move; past that point it becomes a trap. Decision cost is itself a design knob — high cost makes choices rare and deep, low cost makes them frequent and shallow

intro.what: Each round offers you a few options — pick one and live with the consequences. Card battlers, auto-chess, and Clash Royale-style tactical choices are built on this.
intro.feel: Three rewards sit in front of you, each tempting and each with a price; you weigh them forever, pick one, and rounds later that choice starts paying off — or biting back.
intro.why: "Meaningful choice" is the soul of strategy games — fake choices, information volume, and consequence explanation are all laid bare here.

concept: Choice-based strategy wraps "randomness" as "governable fate": options are limited and consequences traceable, so players believe outcomes were chosen by themselves. The hard part is not the number of options — it is the explainability of their differences: converging payoffs degenerate into fake choices, too much information causes decision fatigue, too little turns play into guessing. The player’s sense of "strategy" rests on being able to replay and trace every choice afterward.
designNotes: A fake choice is worse than no choice: three options with converging net value make players feel fooled — option differences must land on explainable numbers, or the selection ritual is just dice-rolling.
Reroll is a gentle trap: trading a fixed cost for better options is rational while cost ≤ benefit, and a resource black hole beyond that — decision cost is itself the knob most worth tuning.
Risk must be visible to accumulate: making risk an explicit metric lets players feel the fragility of a single-track strategy — invisible risk never becomes strategy, only complaints.
